/world/2026/oct/11/zelenskyy-trump-ukrai.headline: Zelenskyy offers to halt refinery strikes, hold elections for 60-day truce
/world/2026/oct/11/zelenskyy-trump-ukrai.bodyHtml:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready to accept an energy ceasefire with Russia, after Donald Trump announced a unilateral deal to halt the two countries’ long-range attacks that the Ukrainian president said was “news to me”.

Trump made the claim in a social media post, saying the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.

Zelenskyy said he would agree to the ceasefire if Vladimir Putin did the same, telling the Axios website: “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it.” He said he was surprised by the announcement, which Trump had made with no further details.

Zelenskyy had earlier said Moscow would have to halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure before Kyiv would stop bombing Russian oil refineries, as Trump had demanded on Saturday.

He said any deal to end Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes on Russian targets would have to be “reciprocal” and backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.

Zelenskyy said Russian drones had filled the skies “throughout the day” on Sunday, with “unfortunately” several airstrikes also hitting energy infrastructure, as the Kremlin gave no sign it was observing Trump’s ceasefire.

He said Russian forces had hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv, the latest of more than 200 strikes this week on Ukraine’s electricity generation and transmission facilities, with another 17 hits on gas and oil sites.

The dispute between Washington and Kyiv had begun on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move he said would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. Trump responded that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries, saying on Saturday that Ukraine needed a “new leader”.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”, telling ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and organise elections – but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office last year.

The Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe, that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that supplies Ukraine with weapons, in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire, The New York Times has reported, including releasing billions in frozen Russian sovereign assets. The Trump administration has also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil, in a multibillion deal the paper reported would benefit Middle Eastern investors, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.

Zelenskyy laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”, after Trump criticised him on Saturday and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” Zelenskyy said.

In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres. Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding they give up this, their most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia.

Russia’s own bombing campaign has continued. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign, involving thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones, continued “unabated”.

Oleksandr Merezhko, the head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had “paradoxically” strengthened him at home, despite recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.

He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”

Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”

Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine. He acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.

Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support among key allies in a series of calls, including with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Earlier, Zelenskyy had spoken with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.

Downing Street said the two leaders had agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary, adding in a statement: “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea.”

Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision had empowered Putin and given him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

  • Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

/world/2026/oct/11/saudi-coalition-retal.headline: Saudi defences intercept missile as allies move to strengthen protection
/world/2026/oct/11/saudi-coalition-retal.bodyHtml:
Saudi air defences intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of Riyadh airport on Sunday, authorities said, as a separate, unidentified projectile struck terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire that killed one person and injured 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.

The intercepted strike and the terminal fire came a day after a deadly missile attack on the same facility, carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group, killed 13 people.

The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.

In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.

After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”

The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.

In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.

The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.

Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.

On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”

On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.

The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.

The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.

“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.

Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.

The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.

Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10 per cent of global maritime goods transit.

It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.

Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60 per cent of whom it said were women and children.

Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.

The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.

The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”

The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war, with governments facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey moved to strengthen their defences on Monday, issuing a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.

The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.

Saudi Arabia has asked France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan for further assistance as its stock of interceptor missiles runs low.

The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.

Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.

Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

The UK is developing a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt hostile state information campaigns aimed at undermining British democracy. Downing Street said it was also working with Germany on a new partnership to counter hybrid threats, including hostile activities that threaten both countries’ security and prosperity.

A spokesperson said: “National security is the first duty of any government – we are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.

“We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies.

“We will continue to leave no stone unturned in our efforts to protect the UK from harm.”

Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.

Andy Burnham sought answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 Brexit referendum as soon as he entered Downing Street, and has now said it is clear Russia interfered in the vote.

Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.

Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”

Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote.

The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.

Parliament’s intelligence and security committee criticised the government and intelligence agencies in a 2020 report for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.

The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.

It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.

The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.

Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.

“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”

He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.

“One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.”

He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”

Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.

/business/2026/oct/12/ifs-budget-report-.headline: IFS sets out Healey’s choices ahead of 28 October budget
/business/2026/oct/12/ifs-budget-report-.bodyHtml:
Britain’s leading tax and spending experts are urging John Healey to set out clear plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures before his budget, saying that without one it risks being seen as a “work of fiction”.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade, as the war in the Middle East and the damage from higher inflation take their toll on the public finances.

The thinktank called on Healey to address the issue at his 28 October budget, warning that against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, failure to do so risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”

Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at the former Conservative chancellor, Jeremy Hunt, who, before the 2024 general election, was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.

In its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances ahead of Healey’s speech to the Commons, the IFS called on the chancellor to make clear choices now rather than announce a “steady as she goes” budget that pushes decisions into next year’s spending review.

“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.

Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”

Miller said an assumption within the Treasury that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.

“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”

Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.

With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.

Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.

The IFS said the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue, meaning that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, Healey’s headroom would be cut by only £4bn.

However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.

Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.

The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.

“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.

“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”

She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

/politics/2026/oct/11/zack-polanski-sign.headline: Zack Polanski calls for Green party democracy to evolve
/politics/2026/oct/11/zack-polanski-sign.bodyHtml:
Zack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction, after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism.

The Green party leader has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation.

Writing for the Guardian after his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion.

Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week.

He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.”

Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction.

“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes.

His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members.

Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged.

The vote that intensified the controversy last weekend saw just 1,022 members – about 0.4% of the party’s total membership – back a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state.

The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution.

Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise the party’s policymaking structures, warning that it must not become vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists.

Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.

“This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion.

“At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic.

“There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.”

The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future.

The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership.

The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.

/technology/2026/oct/12/uk-strengthen-cy.headline: Narayan says UK must build its own AI infrastructure, not rely on tech firms
/technology/2026/oct/12/uk-strengthen-cy.bodyHtml:
Britain is to strengthen its cyber defences, the UK's AI minister will say, as he calls on companies building the most advanced AI systems to increase their safety efforts.

Kanishka Narayan will say the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure and will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe, arguing that Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models.

Narayan's speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK's AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: "The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models."

OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring. Irving cited a recent incident in which the company was "hacked" by cybersecurity researchers, under a programme that rewards ethical hackers for testing its systems; the researchers said "the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge".

Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a "50% chance" of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.

"It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path," he said.

Leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland have already signed a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, and Narayan's speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join them. The UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to "self-police", have not signed. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.

In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.

UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet last week on AI's threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times, a warning some see as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.

The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with "a single set of global principles and standards". Safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.

Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an "emergency brake", saying people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.

"We can't treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions," he wrote. "We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain."

/uk-news/2026/oct/11/tiger-will-not-be-e.headline: Yorkshire wildlife park confirms tiger Altai will not be euthanised
/uk-news/2026/oct/11/tiger-will-not-be-e.bodyHtml:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park has confirmed that the tiger which mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised.

The park said in its statement that the tiger, named Altai, was ‘safe and well and will not be euthanised’ after the incident, adding: ‘The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support.’

Police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday after a man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster.

South Yorkshire police said the tiger ‘subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury’; despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the ‘tragic incident’ and said their ‘thoughts and heartfelt sympathies’ remained with the family of the man who lost his life.

The foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North, Ed Miliband, said he was ‘deeply saddened’ and sent his ‘thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died’.

‘I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,’ Miliband added.

One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was ‘happily enjoying’ his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him.

‘The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,’ the post read.

‘He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.’

Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was ‘frightening and confusing’ when the park was evacuated after the incident.

She said: ‘At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go.

‘The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.’

The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. ‘As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,’ she said. ‘We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.’

South Yorkshire police said the man’s family were being supported by specialist officers after being made aware of the incident on Saturday, and the force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011 on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.
